correctness.rationale: The greedy embedding of the proper prefix sends each predecessor zero block to the least count that forces the indexed next one: shortening a larger count would keep that source one and hence preserve failure. The last block is likewise forced by failure of the terminal letter and the ability to delete one zero. This injects the words into a subset of the k indexed ones plus the terminal bit, giving Pascal's bound including r=0 and k+1. For (010)^k, the initial cost to select source one i is 2(i-1), and a gap d between selected ones costs g(d)=0 for d=1 and 2d-1 otherwise. A zero deletion in a nonfinal positive block permits shifting all following selected ones back one position: the shortened block fits, interior capacities are unchanged, and the tail gains two zeros (or leaves the final source one available). Deleting a selected one between p and q costs at most 2(q-p-1) merged zeros, which fits before q-1. At the beginning the capacity is 2q-3; at the tail after p it is 2(k-p)+1 for a terminal zero and 2(k-p) before the last source one for a terminal one; the witness counts fit these capacities. With no preceding one the corresponding tail capacities are 2k and 2k-1. Final-block zero deletions and deletion of the terminal letter fit by the threshold definition. Thus every code is realized and different codes give distinct words. The frozen verification is finite corroboration, not the basis of this all-k argument; no frozen code was executed.

evidence: Use weights A=sum z^r over words ending in 0, B=sum z^(r-1) over words ending in 1, C=sum z^r over words ending in 00. The same-letter append replacement appends that letter to the old absent word. For appending 1 already present, the rules give B'=zB, A'<=A+zB, C'<=A coefficientwise. For appending 0 already present, A'=A; B gains nothing after a 0, gains C after a single terminal 1, and gains A after a terminal run of at least two ones.

Inductively A,B<=(1+z)^k; on a word ending in 1 also B<=z(1+z)^(k-1), C<=(1+z)^(k-1). The displayed update proves the induction on a 1. On a 0 after a single terminal 1 use the two stronger bounds; after a longer run A is unchanged from the prefix with one fewer 1, giving A<=(1+z)^(k-1). On 0^m one has A=B=1. At the first 1, B=z, A<=1+z and C<=1; at the first 0 after 1^k the polynomials are A=1, B=1+z^k. These are the original proof's boundary cases with weights.

On (010)^1, A=B=1+z and C=A. In the original witness induction append 010: the initial 0 preserves A,B and the 00 suffix property; the 1 gives A'=A+zB, B'=zB, C'=A; the final 0 then gives B''=zB+A and restores C''=A''. Consequently A=B=(1+z)^k on the witness. The unconditioned weight A+zB gives the upper bound and equality layer by layer.
